problem: The complex pair with ζ=0.4 and ωn=5 rad/s has real part −2 s⁻¹. The extra real pole at −0.5 s⁻¹ is closer to the imaginary axis, so by the standard dominant-pole rule the real pole is dominant, not the complex pair. Calling the complex pair dominant contradicts the definition and can mislead students.
fix: Either move the extra real pole far left (for example to −20 s⁻¹) if the complex pair is meant to dominate, or reword Q7: the real pole at −0.5 s⁻¹ is actually the dominant pole, so all second-order pair estimates may fail; settling is then dominated by the slow real pole.

problem: The text says for ζ≥0.707 there is no resonant peak and ωr has no real value. At ζ=0.707 exactly, ωr=0, which is real; the response is maximally flat and has no peak above DC. The 'no real value' wording is only correct for ζ>0.707.
fix: Write: for ζ>0.707 there is no resonant peak and ωr is not defined; at ζ=0.707 the response is maximally flat with ωr=0. Treat ζ≥0.707 as no useful resonance.
